findings.summary: train duplicates: 0 (0.00%); test rows leaking a train feature-match: 0 (0.00%); test-internal duplicates: 0
no feature vector maps to more than one label
no near-zero-distance feature vectors found across 5 classes tested
no single feature or pair dominates importance (top1=12.2%, top2=22.1%)
single rule 'LONGEST_FLOW_PKT <= 34' reaches 90.8% test accuracy (90.8% train)
'SHORTEST_FLOW_PKT' alone reaches AUC 0.990 identifying 'DDoS'; a single feature this separable is worth checking for a leakage artifact
standalone AUC of 'L4_DST_PORT' + 'PROTOCOL' combined: 0.952. Port and protocol together may predict the label without attack behavior
adjacent-row label-transition rate (train=1.00, test=1.01) as a share of what a randomly shuffled ordering would produce
4 classes tested; test-to-train and train-internal proximity statistically indistinguishable for every class (consistent with inherent class homogeneity, not train/test leakage)
5 classes, train imbalance ratio (majority:minority) = 5065:1; classes below 1% of train: ['Benign', 'Theft']
no missing labels, constant features, or +-inf values found

The full dataset is over 99.9% attack traffic (benign flows are 129,437 of 30,420,086 rows, 0.43%), an order of magnitude more skewed than most NIDS datasets; a uniform row-level sample may carry very few or zero benign rows, and a classifier's accuracy on this data mostly reflects its attack-vs-attack discrimination, not its ability to recognize normal traffic. (Koroniotis et al. 2019, Future Generation Computer Systems)
